title: BlindEagle Targeting Ecuador With Sharpened Tools

attributes.evidence_span: APT-C-36, also known as Blind Eagle, is a financially motivated threat group that has been launching indiscriminate attacks against citizens of various countries in South America since at least 2018.

evidences.text: APT-C-36, also known as Blind Eagle, is a financially motivated threat group that has been launching indiscriminate attacks against citizens of various countries in South America since at least 2018.
In a recent campaign targeting Ecuador based organizations, CPR detected a new infection chain that involves a more advanced toolset.
The backdoor chosen for this campaign is typically used by espionage campaigns, which is unusual for this group

ACTIVE CAMPAIGNS AGAINST COLOMBIAN TARGETS For the last few months, we have been observing the ongoing campaigns orchestrated by Blind Eagle, which have mostly adhered to the TTPs described above — phishing emails pretending to be from the Colombian government.
QuasarRAT is an open source trojan available in multiple sources like Github.

Although QuasarRAT is not a dedicated banking Trojan, it can be observed from the sample’s embedded strings that the group’s main goal in the campaign was to intercept victim access to their bank account.

A BETTER CAMPAIGN FEATURING NEWER TOOLS One specific sample caught our attention as it was related to a government institution from Ecuador and not from Colombia.
Similarly to the campaign described above, the geo-filter server in this campaign redirects requests outside of Ecuador and Colombia to the website of the Ecuadorian Internal Revenue Service:
If contacted from Colombia or Ecuador, the downloaded file from Mediafire will be a RAR archive with a password.

This code just adds a new stage in the infection chain: ctypes.windll.user32.ShowWindow(ctypes.windll.kernel32.GetConsoleWindow(), 0) os.system(wsx) mshta is a utility that executes Microsoft HTML Applications, and the attackers abuse it here to download and execute the next stage, which contains VBS code embedded in an HTML.

<script language="VBScript"> self.close </script> Usually campaigns by Blind Eagle abuse legitimate file sharing services such as Mediafire or free dynamic domains like “*.linkpc.net”; this case is different, and the next stage is hosted at the malicious domain upxsystems[.]com.
For Windows 7 the task will be created by downloading an XML from the C2 “upxsystems[.]com”, while for Windows 8, 8.1, and 10 the malware will create the task using the cmdlet “New-ScheduledTask*”.
CONCLUSION Blind Eagle is a strange bird among APT groups.

This latest campaign targeting Ecuador highlights how, over the last few years, Blind Eagle has matured as a threat — refining their tools, adding features to leaked code bases, and experimenting with elaborate infection chains and “Living off the Land” as seen with the clever abuse of mshta .
